prompt: How is pyrrole obtained commercially?

choices.text: By treating furan with ammonia over an alumina catalyst at 400 °C
By acid-catalyzed dehydration of five-carbon sugars
choices.why: That's how furan is obtained, from oat hulls and corncobs. Furan is then converted into pyrrole with ammonia.

choices.text: By Hofmann elimination of pyrrolidine
choices.why: Hofmann elimination opens a saturated nitrogen ring. It isn't how pyrrole is made.

choices.text: By nitration of 1,3-cyclopentadiene followed by reduction
choices.why: Nitration and reduction are used to make arylamines. Pyrrole comes from furan and ammonia.

explanation: Pyrrole, the simplest five-membered unsaturated heterocyclic amine, is obtained commercially by treating furan with ammonia over an alumina catalyst at 400 °C. Furan, its oxygen analog, comes from acid-catalyzed dehydration of the five-carbon sugars in oat hulls and corncobs.

prompt: What is the pK_a of the pyrrolinium ion, the protonated form of pyrrole?
explanation: The pK_a of the pyrrolinium ion is 0.4, so pyrrole, unlike most other amines, is not basic. Its saturated counterpart, pyrrolidine, has an ammonium-ion pK_a of 11.27 (Table 24.3.1).

prompt: How many π electrons does the aromatic ring of pyrrole contain?
explanation: Each of the four carbons contributes one π electron, and the sp2-hybridized nitrogen contributes two more from its lone pair: 4 + 2 = 6, an aromatic sextet.

prompt: How many π electrons does the nitrogen atom of pyrrole contribute to the aromatic sextet?
explanation: Pyrrole's sp2-hybridized nitrogen contributes the two electrons of its lone pair to the π system, and the four carbons contribute one each. Because the lone pair is part of the sextet, pyrrole is not basic.

prompt: Why is pyrrole's nitrogen so much less basic than the nitrogen of an aliphatic amine?

choices.text: Protonation would destroy the ring's aromaticity
Its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring
choices.why: That describes pyridine, whose lone pair is outside the π system. Pyridine is a real, if weak, base (pK_a 5.25).

choices.text: It has no lone pair, because it forms four bonds
choices.why: Pyrrole's nitrogen forms three bonds and has a lone pair. The lone pair is tied up in the aromatic π system.

choices.text: Its nitrogen is sp3-hybridized and holds the lone pair tightly
choices.why: Pyrrole's nitrogen is sp2-hybridized, and its lone pair is part of the aromatic π system.

explanation: Because the nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, protonation on nitrogen would destroy the aromaticity of the ring. So pyrrole's nitrogen is less electron-rich, less basic, and less nucleophilic than the nitrogen of an aliphatic amine.

prompt: Pyrrole looks like a conjugated diene. How does it react with electrophiles?

choices.text: It undergoes substitution, not addition, because it is aromatic
It undergoes 1,4-addition, like other conjugated dienes
choices.why: Unlike most conjugated dienes, pyrrole gives substitution, which keeps the aromatic ring intact.

choices.text: It doesn't react with electrophiles at all
choices.why: Pyrrole is more reactive toward electrophiles than benzene; low temperatures are often needed to control the reactions.

choices.text: It reacts only at nitrogen, forming a stable salt
choices.why: Pyrrole isn't basic. Its electron-rich carbons are where electrophiles react.

explanation: Unlike most conjugated dienes, pyrrole undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions rather than additions, because it has six π electrons and is aromatic. Halogenation, nitration, sulfonation, and Friedel–Crafts acylation can all be carried out.

prompt: How do the carbon atoms of pyrrole compare with typical double-bond carbons, such as those of 1,3-cyclopentadiene?

choices.text: They are more electron-rich and more nucleophilic
They are less electron-rich, because nitrogen withdraws electrons from them
choices.why: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the ring, which makes the carbons more electron-rich.

choices.text: They are about the same in electron density
choices.why: Electrostatic potential maps show that pyrrole's carbons are more electron-rich (more red) than those of 1,3-cyclopentadiene.

choices.text: They are positively polarized, like the ring carbons of pyridine
choices.why: Pyridine's ring carbons are the positive end of its dipole. Pyrrole's carbons are electron-rich.

explanation: Because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the ring, pyrrole's carbon atoms are more electron-rich and more nucleophilic than typical double-bond carbons, and the ring reacts with electrophiles in the same way as enamines. Overall, these heterocycles are more reactive toward electrophiles than benzene rings.

prompt: Pyrrole reacts with Br2 at 0 °C. What is the major product?

choices.text: 2-Bromopyrrole
3-Bromopyrrole
choices.why: Substitution at position 3 goes through a less stable cation with only two resonance forms.

choices.text: 1-Bromopyrrole, with bromine on nitrogen
choices.why: Electrophiles attack pyrrole's electron-rich carbons, not its nonbasic nitrogen.

choices.text: An addition product with no remaining aromatic ring
choices.why: Pyrrole is aromatic and undergoes substitution, not addition.

explanation: Electrophilic substitutions of pyrrole normally occur at position 2, next to the nitrogen. Bromination at 0 °C gives 2-bromopyrrole in 92% yield.

prompt: Electrophilic attack at position 2 of pyrrole, next to the nitrogen, gives an intermediate cation with how many resonance forms?
explanation: Reaction at position 2 gives a more stable intermediate cation with three resonance forms, whereas reaction at position 3 gives a less stable cation with only two (Figure 24.9.1). That's why substitution normally occurs next to the nitrogen.

prompt: Imidazole, a constituent of the amino acid histidine, has two nitrogen atoms. How many of them are basic?
explanation: Imidazole has two nitrogens, only one of which is basic. Thiazole, another five-membered heterocycle, also contains a basic nitrogen, which is alkylated in thiamin (vitamin B1).

prompt: Pyridine, like benzene, is flat and aromatic. What is the length of its C–C bonds, in picometers?
explanation: Pyridine has bond angles of 120° and C–C bond lengths of 139 pm, intermediate between typical single and double bonds.

prompt: Where is the nitrogen lone pair of pyridine?

choices.text: In an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring
In a p orbital, as part of the aromatic sextet
choices.why: That describes pyrrole. In pyridine, the nitrogen contributes one π electron, like each carbon, and its lone pair stays in the plane of the ring.

choices.text: In an sp3 orbital, as in an alkylamine
choices.why: Pyridine's nitrogen is sp2-hybridized.

choices.text: Spread evenly over all six ring atoms
choices.why: The lone pair stays on nitrogen, in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring.

explanation: The five carbon atoms and the sp2-hybridized nitrogen of pyridine each contribute one π electron to the aromatic sextet, and the nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring.

prompt: How many π electrons does the nitrogen atom of pyridine contribute to the aromatic sextet?
explanation: Pyridine's five carbons and its sp2-hybridized nitrogen each contribute one π electron: 5 + 1 = 6. The nitrogen lone pair lies in an sp2 orbital in the plane of the ring and isn't part of the sextet, unlike pyrrole's.

prompt: Why is pyridine (pK_a 5.25) less basic than an alkylamine?

choices.text: Its lone pair is in an sp2 orbital, with more s character
Its lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet
choices.why: That's the reason for pyrrole. Pyridine's lone pair is outside the π system, in an sp2 orbital.

choices.text: Its lone pair is in an sp3 orbital, which has more s character
choices.why: An sp3 orbital has less s character (25%) than an sp2 orbital (33%), and pyridine's nitrogen is sp2.

choices.text: Its ring nitrogen carries a full positive charge
choices.why: Neutral pyridine has no charge on nitrogen.

explanation: The lone-pair electrons on pyridine's nitrogen are in an sp2 orbital, while those on an alkylamine nitrogen are in an sp3 orbital. Electrons in an orbital with more s character are held more closely to the positively charged nucleus and are less available for bonding, so the sp2 nitrogen (33% s character) is less basic than the sp3 nitrogen (25% s character).

prompt: What percentage s character does the sp2 orbital holding pyridine's lone pair have, to the nearest whole percent?
explanation: An sp2 orbital has 33% s character, compared with 25% for the sp3 orbital of an alkylamine nitrogen. The greater s character holds pyridine's lone pair closer to the nucleus, making pyridine the weaker base.

prompt: How does the basicity of pyridine compare with that of pyrrole and of the alkylamines?

choices.text: Pyridine is a stronger base than pyrrole but a weaker base than alkylamines
Pyridine is a weaker base than pyrrole but a stronger base than alkylamines
choices.why: That's reversed: pyridinium's pK_a (5.25) lies between pyrrolinium's (0.4) and the alkylammonium ions' (10 to 11).

choices.text: Pyridine is a stronger base than both
choices.why: Alkylamines are stronger bases: their ammonium ions have pK_a's of 10 to 11.

choices.text: Pyridine is a weaker base than both
choices.why: Pyrrole is weaker still: the pyrrolinium ion's pK_a is only 0.4.

explanation: As Table 24.3.1 shows, pyridine (pK_a 5.25) is a stronger base than pyrrole (pK_a 0.4) but a weaker base than the alkylamines (pK_a 10 to 11).

prompt: Pyridine is treated with Br2 at 300 °C. What is the product?

choices.text: 3-Bromopyridine, in low yield
2-Bromopyridine, in high yield
choices.why: Electrophilic substitution of pyridine is difficult and usually gives the 3-substituted product.

choices.text: 4-Bromopyridine
choices.why: The intermediates from attack at positions 2 and 4 are unfavorable (Exercise 24.9.3). Reaction gives the 3-substituted product.

choices.text: 2,4,6-Tribromopyridine, rapidly
choices.why: Unlike aniline, pyridine reacts with electrophiles only with difficulty; drastic conditions give a 3-substituted product.

explanation: Unlike benzene, pyridine undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution only with difficulty, and reactions usually give the 3-substituted product. Bromination at 300 °C gives 3-bromopyridine in 30% yield.

prompt: Which pair of factors makes pyridine unreactive toward electrophilic aromatic substitution?

choices.text: Nitrogen complexes the electrophile and withdraws electrons inductively
The ring isn't aromatic, and the nitrogen lone pair is part of the π system
choices.why: Pyridine is aromatic, and its lone pair is not part of the π system.

choices.text: The ring carbons are so electron-rich that they repel electrophiles
choices.why: The ring carbons are the positive end of pyridine's dipole. They are electron-poor.

choices.text: The ring is strained and its C–C bonds are too short
choices.why: Pyridine is flat with 120° angles, like benzene, and its C–C bonds (139 pm) are typical of an aromatic ring.

explanation: Acid–base complexation between the basic ring nitrogen and the incoming electrophile places a positive charge on the ring, deactivating it. Equally important, the electronegative nitrogen withdraws electron density from the ring by its inductive effect, giving pyridine a dipole moment of 2.26 D with the ring carbons as the positive end.

prompt: What is the dipole moment of pyridine, in debyes?
explanation: Pyridine has a substantial dipole moment, μ = 2.26 D, with the ring carbons as the positive end. Reaction of an electrophile with these positively polarized carbons is therefore difficult.

prompt: Why is pyrimidine (pK_a 1.3) substantially less basic than pyridine (pK_a 5.25)?

choices.text: The second ring nitrogen withdraws electrons by its inductive effect
Its nitrogen lone pairs are part of the aromatic sextet, as in pyrrole
choices.why: Pyrimidine is a six-membered ring like pyridine. Its weaker basicity is due to the inductive effect of the second nitrogen.

choices.text: It isn't aromatic
choices.why: Pyrimidine is aromatic, like pyridine.

choices.text: Its nitrogens are sp3-hybridized
choices.why: sp3 nitrogens, as in alkylamines, are more basic, not less. Pyrimidine's nitrogens are sp2, like pyridine's.

explanation: Pyrimidine, the six-membered diamine found in nucleic acids, has pK_a 1.3 and is substantially less basic than pyridine because of the inductive effect of the second nitrogen.

prompt: Quinoline is brominated with Br2 in H2SO4. Where does substitution occur?

choices.text: On the benzene ring, at positions 5 and 8
On the pyridine ring, giving only 3-bromoquinoline
choices.why: Reaction occurs on the benzene ring, not on the nitrogen-containing ring, and gives a mixture.

choices.text: On the nitrogen, giving an N-bromo salt
choices.why: Substitution occurs on carbon atoms of the benzene ring.

choices.text: Nowhere, because quinoline is too unreactive
choices.why: Quinoline is less reactive than benzene, but it does undergo electrophilic substitution.

explanation: Quinoline and isoquinoline have basic, pyridine-like nitrogens and are less reactive than benzene toward electrophilic substitution. Reaction occurs on the benzene ring rather than the pyridine ring, and a mixture is obtained: 5- and 8-bromoquinoline.

prompt: Indole reacts with Br2 in dioxane at 0 °C. What is the product?

choices.text: 3-Bromoindole
2-Bromoindole
choices.why: Indole reacts at position 3. Attack at position 2 would cost the benzene ring its aromaticity in the intermediate.

choices.text: A bromoindole substituted on the benzene ring
choices.why: Substitution occurs on the electron-rich pyrrole ring, not on the benzene ring.

choices.text: 1-Bromoindole, with bromine on nitrogen
choices.why: Indole's nitrogen is nonbasic and pyrrole-like. The electrophile attacks a ring carbon.

explanation: Indole has a nonbasic, pyrrole-like nitrogen and undergoes electrophilic substitution more easily than benzene. Substitution occurs at position 3 of the electron-rich pyrrole ring, giving 3-bromoindole.

prompt: Why does indole react with electrophiles at position 3 rather than position 2?

choices.text: Attack at position 2 costs the benzene ring its aromaticity
Position 3 is the one next to the nitrogen
choices.why: Position 2 is next to the nitrogen. Position 3 is one atom farther away.

choices.text: Position 3 is on the benzene ring, which is more reactive
choices.why: Position 3 is on the five-membered, pyrrole-like ring.

choices.text: Position 2 is blocked by the hydrogen on the ring nitrogen
choices.why: Nothing blocks position 2. Attack there is disfavored because the intermediate loses the benzene ring's aromaticity.

explanation: Drawing resonance forms of the intermediate cations shows that reaction at position 2 is disfavored because the aromaticity of the benzene ring is lost (Exercise 24.9.5). Note the contrast with pyrrole, which reacts next to the nitrogen.

prompt: Purine has four nitrogen atoms. How many of them are basic, pyridine-like nitrogens?
explanation: Purine has three basic, pyridine-like nitrogens with lone pairs in sp2 orbitals in the plane of the ring. The remaining nitrogen is nonbasic and pyrrole-like, with its lone pair part of the aromatic π electron system.

prompt: N,N-Dimethyltryptamine is an indole alkaloid with a –CH2CH2N(CH3)2 side chain on the indole ring. Which of its nitrogens is more basic?

choices.text: The side-chain nitrogen
The indole ring nitrogen
choices.why: Indole's ring nitrogen is pyrrole-like and nonbasic: its lone pair is part of the aromatic π system.

choices.text: Both are equally basic
choices.why: The ring nitrogen's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet, while the side-chain nitrogen's lone pair is free to accept a proton.

choices.text: Neither is basic
choices.why: The side-chain nitrogen is an alkylamine nitrogen with an available lone pair, so it is basic.

explanation: The side-chain nitrogen is more basic than the ring nitrogen (Exercise 24.9.4). Indole has a nonbasic, pyrrole-like nitrogen whose lone pair is part of the aromatic π system, while the side-chain N(CH3)2 is an ordinary tertiary alkylamine nitrogen.
